subject: Vocabulary
topic: Idioms Using Body Parts — Meaning in Context (W12 B1)

questions.stem: The security guard was asked to KEEP AN EYE ON the new employee. What does this mean?

options.option_text: to stare at constantly
to watch or monitor carefully
to teach and train someone
to ignore completely

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Keep an eye on' = to watch or monitor someone/something carefully, usually to prevent problems. 'Stare at constantly' would imply rudeness — the idiom implies discreet observation. Use: 'Keep an eye on the luggage while I buy tickets.' Trap: 'ignore' = the opposite; 'teach' = nothing in the idiom suggests training.

questions.stem: When her children kept playing video games past midnight, she finally PUT HER FOOT DOWN. What does this mean?

options.option_text: She stamped her foot in frustration
She firmly refused to allow it any further
She joined them in playing games
She walked away without saying anything

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Put one's foot down' = to firmly insist on something or refuse to allow something; to take a firm stand. The phrase conveys authority and finality. Use: 'The principal put his foot down on mobile phones in classrooms.' Trap: 'stamped in frustration' = a literal (and wrong) reading; physical frustration is not what the idiom means; 'walked away' = the opposite of asserting authority.

questions.stem: He was confident about the interview all week, but got COLD FEET at the last minute. What does this expression mean?

options.option_text: his feet literally turned cold from the weather
he was suddenly overcome by nervousness or fear
he left the venue without completing the interview
he became very focused and composed

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Get cold feet' = to suddenly lose confidence or courage just before doing something; to become nervous and hesitant at the last moment. Use: 'She had planned to sing on stage but got cold feet.' Trap: 'left without completing' = a possible consequence of getting cold feet, but not the meaning of the idiom itself; 'became focused' = the opposite of nervousness.

questions.stem: Even though the medical procedure was very painful, the patient decided to BITE THE BULLET and go through with it. What does this mean?

options.option_text: to refuse treatment out of fear
to endure a painful or unpleasant situation with courage
to seek a second medical opinion
to complain loudly throughout the ordeal

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Bite the bullet' = to endure a painful or difficult situation stoically, without complaint. Historical origin: before anesthesia, soldiers undergoing surgery were given a bullet to bite to manage the pain. Use: 'Just bite the bullet and apologise — it'll make things better.' Trap: 'refuse out of fear' = the opposite (biting the bullet means going through with it despite fear); 'complain loudly' = the idiom specifically implies NOT complaining.

questions.stem: The manager TURNED A BLIND EYE to the minor rule-breaking because it didn't affect productivity. What does this mean?

options.option_text: he made a note of it for future reference
he deliberately chose to ignore it
he punished the rule-breaker publicly
he temporarily lost his sight from stress

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Turn a blind eye (to something)' = to deliberately ignore or overlook something you know is happening, choosing not to act on it. Origin: attributed to Admiral Horatio Nelson who, during the Battle of Copenhagen, put his telescope to his blind eye to avoid seeing the signal to retreat. Use: 'The teacher turned a blind eye to students whispering during break.' Trap: 'made a note for future' = the opposite of ignoring; 'punished publicly' = the opposite of turning a blind eye.

questions.stem: Before the actor went on stage for his debut performance, his director told him: 'Break a leg!' What did the director mean?

options.option_text: be careful not to fall on stage
good luck with your performance
give such a powerful performance it shocks the audience
try a dangerous stunt for extra applause

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Break a leg!' = a theatrical idiom meaning 'good luck', used especially to performers before they go on stage. The phrase is used as a superstition — saying 'good luck' directly is considered bad luck in theatre, so this contrary expression substitutes. Use: 'Your recital starts in ten minutes — break a leg!' Trap: 'be careful not to fall' = literal and opposite meaning; 'give a shocking performance' = not related to the idiom's meaning.

questions.stem: The designer handbag COST HER AN ARM AND A LEG, but she bought it anyway. What does this expression mean?

options.option_text: it caused her physical pain to carry
it was extremely expensive
it required a great deal of effort to find
it was cheaply acquired

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Cost an arm and a leg' = to be very expensive; to cost an unreasonably high price (implying you'd have to give up body parts to afford it). Use: 'Repairing this antique clock cost an arm and a leg.' Trap: 'physical pain to carry' = literal misreading (handbags don't literally cause limb loss); 'required great effort to find' = effort, not cost, is different; 'cheaply acquired' = the opposite.

questions.stem: Could you please GIVE ME A HAND with moving this heavy sofa? What does this idiom mean?

options.option_text: literally hold my hand for support
applaud me as a gesture of appreciation
help me with this task
hand over a tool to me

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Give someone a hand' = to help someone with a task. Use: 'Can you give me a hand carrying these boxes?' Also: 'Give someone a (big) hand' = to applaud someone. The context (moving a sofa) makes the 'help' meaning clear over the 'applause' meaning. Trap: 'applaud' = another valid meaning of 'give a hand' but the context here is physical help (moving a sofa), not a performance situation.

questions.stem: Despite losing his job, he tried to KEEP HIS CHIN UP and stay positive. What does this expression mean?

options.option_text: to maintain good posture under pressure
to remain cheerful and brave in a difficult situation
to confront a problem directly and aggressively
to hide his emotions from others

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Keep one's chin up' = to remain cheerful, brave and optimistic during a difficult time; to not let adversity defeat you emotionally. Often used as encouragement: 'Keep your chin up — things will get better soon!' Origin: drooping chin = sadness; raised chin = confidence/resilience. Trap: 'maintain posture' = literal reading; 'confront aggressively' = 'chin up' is about inner resilience, not outward aggression; 'hide emotions' = stoic concealment, but chin-up implies genuine positive attitude.

questions.stem: The employee told his micromanaging supervisor: 'You need to GET OFF MY BACK about the deadline — I'm handling it.' What does 'get off my back' mean?

options.option_text: stop following me around the office
help me carry the workload instead of criticising
stop criticising or pressuring me
step aside and let me take the lead

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Get off someone's back' = to stop criticising, nagging, or putting pressure on someone. Also phrased as: 'Get someone off your back' = to stop someone from bothering you. Use: 'I wish my boss would get off my back about the sales targets.' Origin: the image of someone riding or pressing down on your back (a burden = persistent criticism). Trap: 'stop following' = surveillance is different from criticism; 'step aside' = the idiom is about stopping pressure, not about yielding authority.
